books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls Convention, 1848

stimulus.source_note: Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls Convention, July 1848. Public domain.
stimulus.text: He has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns. He has compelled her to submit to laws, in the formation of which she had no voice.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The grievance about property and wages most directly describes the legal condition known as

options.text: popular sovereignty in the Western territories.
options.misconception: Background from the books: popular sovereignty let territorial settlers vote on slavery; it has nothing to do with married women’s property.

options.text: the free-labor ideal of Northern wage workers.
options.misconception: Background from the books: free labor promised Northern workers the fruits of their own work; the grievance shows married women denied exactly that.
Background from the books: nullification was a state’s claim to void federal law; the grievance concerns a wife’s rights, not a state’s powers.

options.text: coverture, husbands controlling wives’ property and earnings.

rationales.A: Background from the books: popular sovereignty let territorial settlers vote on slavery; it has nothing to do with married women’s property.
rationales.B: Background from the books: free labor promised Northern workers the fruits of their own work; the grievance shows married women denied exactly that.
rationales.C: Background from the books: nullification was a state’s claim to void federal law; the grievance concerns a wife’s rights, not a state’s powers.
rationales.D: Background from the books: a wife who cannot keep her own wages lives under coverture, the law that folds her legal identity into her husband’s.
rationales.general:
1. Read the grievance plainly: her property is taken, even the wages she earns.
2. Background from the books: marriage law gave husbands control of wives’ property and earnings.
3. Name that law: coverture, the rule that a married woman had no separate legal standing.
Remember: when a grievance lists what someone cannot own, find the law that takes it.
